extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (particularly those studying Kant and Schopenhauer)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository/philosophical guidance and doctrinal claims from Schopenhauer about how to understand Kant, what counts as true philosophy, and the nature of the world as 'idea' (with related methodological warnings for students and professors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Kantian philosophy as prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in this way can any one become susceptible to the more positive expositions which I have to give. On the other hand, he who has not mastered the Kantian philosophy ... is, as it were, in a state of innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer insists that a proper understanding of his subsequent expositions requires prior mastery of Kant; cursory lectures or second-hand accounts leave one in a 'natural and childish realism' unsuited to philosophy. He implies that serious students must study Kant directly and not rely on superficial summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Kant from Kant's own works
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kantian doctrine then will be sought for in vain anywhere else but in Kant’s own works; but these are throughout instructive, even where he errs, even where he fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit warning against learning Kant through others' expositions (especially recent Hegelian accounts). Schopenhauer stresses that extraordinary intellects must be known from their own works because their thoughts lose power when 'filtered through the vulgar mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Hegelian and second‑hand expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: I have met with expositions of the Kantian philosophy in the writings of the Hegelians which actually reach the incredible. How should the minds that in the freshness of youth have been strained and ruined by the nonsense of Hegelism, be still capable of following Kant’s profound investigations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He cautions that exposure to bombastic or fashionable expositions (e.g., Hegelian sophistries) warps understanding, producing pretentiousness and sophistry; such readers may need a 'medicina mentis' before they can approach serious philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: True philosophical teaching comes from original texts, not popular accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: One can only come to know them from their own works, not from the accounts of others. For the thoughts of any extraordinary intellect cannot stand being filtered through the vulgar mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruction: students drawn to philosophy should seek out the immortal teachers in the 'still sanctuary of their works'; principal chapters of true philosophers afford far more insight than heavy, distorted second‑hand accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware professional incentives that shape academic philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: These gentlemen desire to live, and indeed to live by philosophy. To philosophy they are assigned with their wives and children... the fear of the Lord, the will of the ministry, the laws of the established church, the wishes of the publisher, the attendance of the students, the goodwill of colleagues, the course of current politics...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer diagnoses a systemic bias: university/professional philosophy often conforms to external aims (livelihood, church, politics, publishers) and thus resists or ignores philosophies that do not serve those aims. This is both descriptive and a warning to readers about institutional distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected professional 'procedure' toward inconvenient philosophies
rubrics_metrics.description: This procedure ... consists, as is well known, in altogether ignoring and thus in secreting—according to Goethe’s malicious phrase, which just means the appropriating of what is of weight and significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He describes the common tactic among professors of ignoring new work while quietly appropriating parts useful to them, often masking this by loud self‑congratulation; advice (implicit) to be wary of such silent suppression and to guard young indiscreet advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy aimed solely at truth may lack professional viability
rubrics_metrics.description: My philosophy is by no means so constituted that any one can live by it. It lacks the first indispensable requisite of a well-paid professional philosophy, a speculative theology...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer contrasts his 'quiet, earnest search for truth' with professional philosophies that furnish speculative theology or other consolations acceptable to institutions; implication: rigorous truth‑seeking may be uncompromising and unrewarded in institutional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should offer insight only to truth‑seekers, not to parties
rubrics_metrics.description: No one reaps any benefit from my works but the man who seeks the truth alone, and therefore none of the philosophical parties of the day; for they all follow their own aims, while I have only insight into truth to offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative stance about the audience of genuine philosophy: it speaks to solitary truth‑seekers rather than to groups pursuing personal or political ends; this functions as a criterion for assessing whether a work is 'true philosophy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Start analysis by regarding presented objects as ideas (world as idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The world is my idea’—this is a truth which holds good for everything that lives and knows... what he knows is not a sun and an earth, but only an eye that sees a sun, a hand that feels an earth; that the world which surrounds him is there only as idea, i.e. only in relation to something else, the consciousness, which is himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rule for philosophical inquiry in this book: treat all presented objects (including one's own body) as ideas—objects relative to a perceiving subject—abstaining (for the moment) from consideration of will. This is an a priori foundational starting point for subsequent analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the principle of sufficient reason to unify forms (time, space, causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: I maintain that the principle of sufficient reason is the general expression for all these forms of the object of which we are a priori conscious; and that therefore all that we know purely a priori, is merely the content of that principle and what follows from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer directs that analyses of space, time, and causality should be understood as specific manifestations of the broader principle of sufficient reason; this functions as a theoretical standard for treating a priori knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ideas of perception from abstract ideas (reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief distinction among our ideas is that between ideas of perception and abstract ideas. The latter form just one class of ideas, namely concepts, and these are the possession of man alone... The first, simplest, and ever-present example of understanding is the perception of the actual world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for conceptual analysis: when examining mental content separate sensory/perceptual ideas from conceptual/abstract ideas (reason/concepts), since they have different origins, functions, and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is intellectual and presupposes a priori knowledge of causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is not merely of the senses, but intellectual—that is, pure knowledge through the understanding of the cause from the effect, and that, consequently, it presupposes the law of causality... The contrary doctrine that the law of causality results from experience... is refuted by this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer claims as a methodological/epistemic criterion that genuine perception already involves understanding the cause from the effect; thus causality is a precondition (a priori) for perception and experience, not a posteriori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate subject–object relation with cause–effect relation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is needful to guard against the grave error of supposing that because perception arises through the knowledge of causality, the relation of subject and object is that of cause and effect. For this relation subsists only between the immediate object and objects known indirectly, thus always between objects alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical warning: even though understanding makes perception by inferring causes from effects, the metaphysical relation between subject and object is not one of causation; keep these relations distinct in philosophical argumentation to avoid skeptical confusions about reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of matter: treat matter as causation/action with derived properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter is nothing more than causation... The existence of matter is therefore entirely relative... These unalterable characteristics are space-occupation, i.e., impenetrability, i.e., causal action, consequently, extension, infinite divisibility, persistence, i.e., indestructibility, and lastly mobility: weight, on the other hand... must be attributed to a posteriori knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing physical reality philosophically, consider matter's essence as active causation; many of its properties (extension, impenetrability, divisibility, persistence, mobility) follow from the forms of our a priori knowledge (space and time), while some (e.g., weight) are empirical.
